content: The alpha effect describes the phenomenon where a molecule exhibits increased nucleophilicity due to the presence of an adjacent (alpha) atom that possesses lone pair electrons. Importantly, this increased nucleophilicity does not necessarily correlate with an increase in basicity when compared to a similar molecule lacking the adjacent electron-donating atom. This effect has been extensively studied, and while numerous theories have been proposed to explain it, no single explanation has been universally accepted. The alpha effect was first identified in 1960 by Jencks and Carriuolo during chemical kinetics experiments involving the reaction of the ester p-nitrophenyl acetate with various nucleophiles. In these experiments, conventional nucleophiles such as the fluoride anion, aniline, pyridine, ethylenediamine, and the phenolate ion demonstrated pseudo-first-order reaction rates that aligned with their basicity, as measured by their pKa values. However, certain other nucleophiles, including the hypochlorite ion, ethanolamine, and the hydroperoxide anion, reacted significantly faster than would be expected based solely on their basicity. In 1962, Edwards and Pearson (the latter known for the Hard and Soft Acids and Bases (HSAB) theory) coined the term alpha effect to describe this anomaly. They suggested that the effect might arise from stabilization of the transition state (TS). Specifically, as the nucleophile enters the transition state, its lone pair of electrons moves away from the nucleus, creating a partial positive charge. This charge can be stabilized by an adjacent lone pair of electrons, similar to the stabilization observed in carbocations. Over the years, additional theories have been proposed to explain the alpha effect. One hypothesis involves ground-state destabilization, where electronic repulsion between the alpha lone pair and the nucleophilic electron pair raises the energy of the ground state, thereby increasing reactivity. Another theory focuses on transition state stabilization, suggesting that the transition state may exhibit free radical character or involve more advanced nucleophile-substrate bond formation. Other factors, such as the polarizability of the nucleophile or the involvement of intramolecular catalysis, have also been implicated. Recent computational studies have provided further insights. One in silico investigation identified a correlation between the alpha effect and the so-called deformation energy, which refers to the electronic energy required to bring the reactants together in the transition state. This finding adds another layer of complexity to our understanding of the alpha effect, highlighting the multifaceted nature of this phenomenon.
